results.title:
AI compute shortage: how bad is it now?
 – Signals Inbox
highlights:
The AI compute shortage is still severe where it matters most: not for a developer renting a few GPUs, but for companies trying to assemble thousands of accelerators, HBM, data-center space and power at once.

Summary

The AI compute shortage is still severe at the top end today: roughly 8/10 for frontier AI companies, while a small developer who only needs a few GPUs is closer to 3/10.

The apparent contradiction is mostly about scale. H100s can be easy to rent one by one while 20,000 newest-generation accelerators, with the right networking, memory, cooling and power, remain very hard to secure as one usable cluster.

The bottleneck has moved deeper into the stack. HBM is extremely tight, more than 80% of new capacity in the main North American data-center markets is already preleased, and grid connections can take far longer than the data centers themselves.

The oddest part is that supply is already expanding at extraordinary speed. North American primary-market capacity grew 33.7% year over year and Microsoft added another gigawatt in a quarter, yet vacancy stayed at 1.4% and Azure demand still ran ahead of capacity.

...

Today's AI compute shortage comes from several bottlenecks piling up at once: advanced accelerators, HBM memory, complete server systems, data-center space and especially electricity.

The easiest mistake is to reduce “compute” to GPUs. Nvidia can manufacture another accelerator, but that accelerator still needs high-bandwidth memory, networking equipment, racks, cooling, a suitable data center and enough electricity to run continuously. A missing component anywhere in that chain can delay usable compute.

The bottleneck has also been moving. GPU availability has improved for smaller buyers. Memory has become much tighter lately. Large data-center projects are running into power constraints. Frontier labs increasingly want hundreds of megawatts or several gigawatts at once, which makes the electricity connection almost as important as the hardware.

That explains why we can simultaneously see H100s available for hourly rental and multi-billion-dollar companies saying they cannot get enough compute. Those customers are buying very different things.

...

## Q8 Can a normal AI startup still rent enough GPUs today?

Usually yes, because the AI compute shortage is much less painful for a startup renting a handful of GPUs than for a company trying to secure an entire AI campus.

Current GPU rental markets are fairly liquid at small scale. Silicon Data's daily market benchmark currently puts an H100 around $2.65 per GPU-hour and a B200 around $5.58. Individual neocloud providers advertise H100, H200 and B200 capacity at similar orders of magnitude.

This changes the practical meaning of “shortage.” A founder who needs four H100s for an experiment can often start quickly. Availability across RunPod, GMI, Lambda, Vast.ai, CoreWeave and other providers has made that part of the market far healthier than during the first H100 rush.

Large clusters behave differently. Prices vary sharply between marketplaces, neoclouds and hyperscalers, and the cheapest capacity may lack the networking, reliability, location or long-term guarantee required for a serious production workload.

Geography adds another complication. Capacity available in one country may be useless to a company that needs European data residency, a particular cloud region or locally hosted sovereign AI infrastructure.

So small-scale GPU access is currently fairly good. The shortage becomes much more obvious once the buyer needs thousands of identical accelerators working together for months.

Current GPU rental market references

| GPU | Rough current market reference | What it tells us |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | ~$2-4 per GPU-hour on many specialty clouds | Small-scale access is fairly easy |
| H200 | ~$2.5-5 per GPU-hour on many specialty clouds | Available, although large blocks are harder |
| B200 | ~$4-7 per GPU-hour across many non-hyperscaler offers | New-generation hardware can already be rented |
| Large dedicated clusters | Usually negotiated privately | Scale, networking and guaranteed duration become the real constraints |

...

Yes, an AI compute glut is a real future risk, although current utilization and capacity data still look much more like shortage than oversupply.

...

The AI compute shortage is still very bad at the top end today: we would rate it around 8/10 for frontier AI companies, while a small developer who needs a few GPUs faces something closer to 3/10.

results.title: Rubin Does Not Obsolete Your GPUs. It Obsoletes Your Building. | Accruex
highlights:
The Uptime Institute’s survey work puts the number plainly. Fewer than 4% of US data centres can support racks above 100kW, and fewer than 1% run them as a standard configuration. Eighty-two per cent of surveyed facilities have a maximum rack density below 30kW, and 9% report a highest-density rack of 50kW or more. Most facilities built over the past decade were designed around roughly 20kW average rack power. [3] 

Most vacant space is the wrong product for a 190–230kW rack.

 Set that against the vacancy picture and the problem sharpens. North American vacancy sits at 1% for the third consecutive year, and most of what is vacant is legacy product that cannot carry the load. In Europe, JLL’s mid-year numbers put FLAP-D vacancy at 6.4% with only 453MW more capacity due to land before year end. [4]

...

The forward curve was already backwardated before CES. Silicon Data’s July prints showed A100 down 15%, H100 down 13% and B200 down 8% across the curve, which is a market pricing more supply and faster obsolescence. [8] On the hardware side, a used eight-GPU H100 system traded at $150,000 to $180,000 in April 2026 against roughly $500,000 for a new B300 server. [6] 

 Underneath that sits the credit market. GPU debt reached investment grade on an assumption that a third-year H100 recovers about 45% of new cost. [9] That residual is not a hardware fact. It is a bet that someone will still want to run the chip at prevailing power prices once something five times faster per package, and considerably better per watt, is generally available. 

 Meanwhile the other price is going the opposite way. Megawatts that can actually host a 230kW rack are scarce in a market at 1% vacancy where fewer than one operator in twenty-five can take the load. Hopper and Blackwell capacity gets cheaper as Rubin lands. Rubin-ready capacity gets dearer, and the two are not substitutes.

results.title: CME Group Will List the First Futures Contracts on AI Computing Power This October. The Benchmark Behind Them Already Prices an Hour of Nvidia's Newest Chip at $5.74. | Pulse24Media
highlights:
CME Group and Silicon Data are about to give Wall Street its first public futures market for Nvidia GPU rental prices, launching October 5. It is a bet that AI compute has finally become standardized enough to trade like oil or wheat, at a moment when the largest cloud providers have committed more than $700 billion to the buildout those chips power.

...

01 CME Group and data provider Silicon Data will launch the first regulated futures contracts on AI computing power on October 5, pending regulatory review, tracking monthly rental costs for Nvidia's H100 and B200 chips on the NYMEX exchange

02 The benchmark already prices an H100 GPU hour at $2.67 and a B200 GPU hour at $5.74, with the B200 rate up 2% over the past week alone

03 Futures markets have historically formed only once an input becomes standardized and liquid, following electricity and natural gas, but a 1989 attempt at DRAM chip futures and 1990s bandwidth trading tied to Enron both collapsed for lack of agreement on what was actually being priced

...

Renting an Nvidia H100 chip for an hour costs $2.67 right now. A B200, Nvidia's newer and more powerful chip, costs $5.74. Until this month those numbers lived inside a specialized pricing service most traders had never heard of. Starting October 5, assuming regulators sign off, they will set the reference price for a public futures market.

CME Group announced the plan alongside Silicon Data, the firm that has spent the past year building daily benchmarks for GPU rental prices across neo-cloud providers and hyperscalers. Pete Keavey, CME's global head of energy and environmental products, said "compute has become the currency of the AI age," and that the new contracts will "bring transparency to current and future costs that AI builders and hyperscalers need to hedge as they grow." The contracts will list on NYMEX, the exchange that already handles crude oil and natural gas futures, and each one will track a full month of GPU rental costs at a time.

results.title: China’s AI Chip Makers Face a New Training-Compute Test · EastFrontier
highlights:
The accessible portion of Caixin’s report describes a market in which demand for AI computing has surged, high-end cards are hard to obtain, and large-cluster capacity has waiting customers. A representative of Zhejiang Computing Power Technology told the publication that its available resources had been fully rented. The company manages 13,000 PFLOPS of intelligent computing capacity, which Caixin says is about 0.6% of China’s national total.

Those figures should be read carefully. They represent the capacity managed by one Zhejiang platform, not a national measure of all AI demand. Still, they point to the practical constraint facing developers: a model-training project requires access not only to individual chips but to many chips operating together, connected by sufficiently fast networks and supported by a compatible software environment.

...

Zhejiang Computing Power Technology is a local state-owned enterprise that builds and aggregates intelligent computing resources, then offers rental capacity to smaller firms at preferential prices, according to Caixin. The company’s 13,000 PFLOPS figure provides a concrete view of what a regional platform can assemble. Its reported full utilization provides an equally concrete warning that demand can outstrip immediately usable supply.

results.title: Neues Geschäftsmodell: Nvidia-Deals mit Rechenzentrenbetreibern vorerst auf Eis | heise online
highlights:
Nvidia setzt seine Pläne für ein neues Geschäftsmodell vorerst nicht weiter um. Das Unternehmen wollte kleinere KI-Infrastrukturbetreiber finanziell unterstützen und im Gegenzug Umsatzbeteiligungen erhalten. Doch dieser Pakt mit Nvidia wäre mit weiteren Verpflichtungen für die Partner gekommen. Einigen Nvidia-Beschäftigten ging das wohl zu weit.

Der Hersteller von KI-Beschleunigern wollte seine massiven Finanzmittel offenbar nutzen, um die weltweit wachsenden Infrastrukturen für KI möglichst weitreichend mit seinen GPUs zu bestücken. Zwar sind die Chips dafür mehr als ausreichend gefragt – der Knackpunkt für potenzielle kleinere Käufer sind aber oft die Preise. Wer seine Rechenzentren damit ausstatten will, steht schnell vor Milliardeninvestitionen. Nvidia erkannte das Problem und startete ein besonderes Programm: Mehrjährige Partnerschaften, bei denen Kunden zunächst Nvidia-GPUs erwerben sollten – unterstützt mit einem Kredit von Nvidia. Die Partner sollten damit dann ihre Rechenzentren bauen, die Kapazität an ihre eigenen Kunden vermieten und dann über einen vorher festgelegten Zeitraum einen Teil ihres Umsatzes an Nvidia abgeben. Der GPU-Hersteller wollte auch das Risiko ausbleibender Kundschaft abfedern: Hätte sich sonst niemand gefunden, hätte er selbst besagte Rechenzentren gemietet.

...

Für diese Kosten hatte Nvidia einen Betrag von 36 Milliarden US-Dollar eingeplant, während die Partnerschaften in der Regel sechs Jahre dauern sollen. Das sagte Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress im Gespräch mit Aktionären, wie das Wall Street Journal (WSJ) berichtet. Was das WSJ noch aus Nvidia-Kreisen erfuhr: Die Partner hätten ihre Kapazitäten für ein paar US-Dollar pro Stunde und GPU an ihre Kunden vermieten sollen, sagten demnach mehreren Personen, die mit der Angelegenheit zu tun hatten. Der Betrag hätte die wesentlichen Kosten decken sollen, inklusive Amortisation der Chips, Fixkosten der Rechenzentren und Personalkosten. Den Mindestpreis für besagte Miete hätten die Partner vorher mit Nvidia aushandeln müssen, was einige Beschäftigte des Unternehmens wohl beunruhigend fanden, wie das WSJ berichtet. Der Ansatz weckte demnach Bedenken, ob sich Nvidia hiermit zu stark in die Geschäfte seiner Kunden einmischt und seine Marktmacht zu sehr ausnutzt. Laut WSJ-Informationen sind die Vorbereitungen für das Programm nun vorerst gestoppt – die exakten Gründe dafür seien aber unbekannt.

results.title: GPU rental prices (H100) end of August?
highlights:
VERDICT: Ornn H100 Index between $3.00 and $3.25 CONFIDENCE: medium

...

The market for high-performance computing, particularly for AI workloads, remains a critical area of focus for technology and finance sectors. At the heart of this market are NVIDIA’s H100 GPUs, which have become the de facto standard for training and deploying large-scale artificial intelligence models. The demand for these accelerators has consistently outstripped supply for an extended period, leading to elevated rental prices across cloud providers and specialized compute platforms.

...

Over the past few weeks, several factors have shaped expectations for H100 rental prices in late 2026. Recent reports from major cloud providers, including Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, indicate a sustained high utilization rate for their H100 GPU clusters. This persistent demand is largely fueled by the continuous development and deployment of large language models and other advanced AI applications across various industries. Enterprise adoption of AI solutions continues to expand, maintaining significant pressure on available compute resources, as highlighted in recent industry analyses from firms like Gartner. This suggests that while supply might be improving, the appetite for H100 compute is not waning.

Furthermore, while NVIDIA’s next-generation Blackwell architecture is beginning its ramp-up, H100 production has also stabilized. Some supply chain analysts suggest a more balanced supply-demand dynamic compared to the extreme scarcity observed in 2024 and early 2025. However, this increased supply is primarily absorbed by existing backlogs and new data center expansions, rather than creating a surplus that would significantly depress prices. For instance, NVIDIA’s Q2 2026 investor calls indicated strong forward bookings for H100s, even with Blackwell on the horizon. Moreover, despite promising performance from competitors like AMD’s MI300X in specific benchmarks, the H100’s mature software ecosystem and established performance profile continue to make it the preferred choice for many mission-critical AI workloads, ensuring its continued relevance and demand.

Considering these dynamics, the range of $3.00 to $3.25 for the Ornn H100 Index appears to be the most justified outcome. This bracket reflects a scenario where the market has absorbed increased H100 supply, but robust demand from enterprise AI and ongoing LLM development prevents any substantial price decline. The alternative range of $2.75 to $3.00, while close, might underestimate the persistent demand and the strategic value cloud providers place on their H100 inventory. A price point below $2.75, such as the $2.50 to $2.75 range, would necessitate a more significant oversupply or a rapid, widespread shift to alternative hardware that current trends do not strongly support. The primary uncertainty remains the exact pace of Blackwell adoption and its impact on H100 demand, alongside any unforeseen breakthroughs in AI model efficiency that could reduce compute requirements.

...

Based on the current trajectory of AI compute demand and supply dynamics, the Ornn H100 Index is most likely to settle between $3.00 and $3.25 on August 31, 2026. Our confidence in this outcome is medium. The core argument rests on the persistent, high-level demand for H100 GPUs, driven by the continuous expansion of enterprise AI applications and the development of increasingly complex large language models. While NVIDIA has worked to alleviate supply constraints, the increased availability has largely been met by existing backlogs and new data center build-outs, preventing a significant downward pressure on rental prices.
